# Coming Clean About the Planet

*Two years writing about air pollution, and what it taught me about why
we keep solving ourselves into new problems*

biteSizedAQ is 2 years old this June!

Two years ago I started biteSizedAQ. The plan was to write easy to
understand posts about complex themes in the air quality literature.
Somewhere along the way the themes got more personal - what it means for
an individual when air quality is bad, not just the city they live in as
a whole. I kept meaning to write about air and kept ending up writing
about the creature breathing it, the one that pollutes and cleans up
after itself in the same afternoon.

So before I go back to charting air pollution, I want to set down where
this has actually taken me — not from above the problem but from inside
it, breathing the same air and making the same compromises I'm about to
pick apart.

In this post, I'll go through a series of behavioral themes and unpick
them to put forward how I understand and view air pollution as an
societal/environmental problem. The conclusions I derive here are more
generally applicable to other fields. These views are my own and may or
may not match your thinking. This post's objective is not to convince
you of my thinking but rather put forward my take on how I view the
human race in the context of general problem solving. The idea is to
identify and address certain forms of hypocrisy so that we can better
understand the problems that arise in front of us and the hope is that
will allow us to take more realistic actions to address them.

## We Want to Survive, Just Not Inconveniently

Most of what humans call "saving the planet" is self-preservation
wearing a better coat. We want to live, but we'd also prefer to ideally
not to give up anything we like in order to do it.

You can watch the pattern repeat for more than a century. We built cars
running on petrol to climb out of a genuine catastrophe, because by the
late 1800s large cities around the world were drowning in horse manure
and everything that bred in it. At the time, the car was the clean
option. Then the exhaust from the clean option turned out to be killing
us slowly, and now we're busy phasing it out. We built air conditioning
to survive heat that genuinely kills, and ran it on enough electricity
to warm the planet we were trying to stay cool on, so now we're shopping
for an alternative to the alternative. Plastics arrived as a miracle,
cheap and sterile and good for everything. Researchers now pull
microplastics out of human placentas. We sprayed DDT on the mosquitoes
that were killing us, then watched it move up the food chain and thin
the eggshells of bald eagles and peregrine falcons until both nearly
blinked out. We split the atom for clean and limitless power, but at a
later point Chernobyl happened, the reactor that melted down and
poisoned a whole region, plus waste that stays dangerous longer than our
entire written history. Fix a thing, break a thing, go again.

Let me be extremely clear - none of this was stupidity. Each move was
the sane choice with the facts available at the time. The manure really
was a public health disaster. Heat really does kill. We don't keep
choosing wrong, exactly. We keep choosing in a hurry, and the cost shows
up later, paid by someone else.

But, what's the alternative then - to not do anything? Of course, NOT.

Answering this clearly is the heart of this post and I'll get into this
in the coming sections.

## The Gap We Paper Over

I want to be careful here, because I'm describing a habit of mind, not
throwing a punch.

Most people don't love the planet. Not the way they say at dinner
parties. If we did, we'd stop, full stop: stop driving, stop flying,
stop eating beef that crossed an ocean to reach the plate, stop
scrolling on a phone built from cobalt and other metals mined, often
brutally, in places like Congo.

We don't stop. We want the convenience and the clean air and the quiet
flattery of thinking ourselves green. We buy the electric car and feel
virtuous and skate right past the lithium mine and the coal plant
feeding the charger. We recycle one yogurt cup and feel like we've made
up for a whole week of throwing things away.

The hypocrisy isn't the harm. It's the gap between what people say they
value and what they actually do, and the story we tell ourselves to
cover that gap. We need to be true to ourselves because otherwise we
have two problems at hand - the dying planet and the untrue individual
trying to save it.

I want to be clear about one thing up front. This is not a tale of
humans as victims. Nobody is being dragged into this against their will.
Look around and you'll find plenty of people who know exactly what
they're doing to the planet and feel nothing about it, working like
pirates: take what you can, bank the profit, leave the wreckage on a
coastline that belongs to someone else. That mode eats its own
foundation; it can't last. The opposite pole is just as useless, though,
the daydream of perfect purity, of some scrubbed humanity that consumes
nothing and touches nothing and floats over the land like a congregation
of saints. A species that turned down every comfort on principle
wouldn't be holy — it would be dead, because refusing all use of the
world is just a slow way of refusing to live in it.

Neither pirate nor saint, then, but somewhere in the awkward middle in
this broad spectrum — and the honest thing to admit is that we haven't
located that middle yet. That isn't weakness of will; it's a hard
problem, and we're still early.

So here is something that people rarely say aloud, which is exactly why
the hypocrisy act keeps running. We are going to keep taking from the
planet. We'll drive and fly and consume and leave marks. And when we do
try to ease up on the harm, we do it for two reasons at the same time,
and the trouble starts the moment we pass one off as the other:

-   Reason one is keeping ourselves alive. We want clean air because
    dirty air kills us. We want a stable climate because the unstable
    kind comes for our houses, our crops, our kids. There's nothing
    noble in it; it's survival, the same reflex that makes you flinch
    from a flame, just stretched across a whole species and a longer
    clock.

-   Reason two is real too, and I won't let the first one swallow it.
    There's a genuine pull (evolutionary or altruistic) in us toward
    being in tune with the living natural world, and it doesn't reduce
    to pure self-interest. People protect animals they'll never eat or
    sell or even lay eyes on. We spend money and pass laws to save a
    far-off marsh, a stretch of reef, a particular birdsong that does
    precisely nothing for our immediate survival. People mourn a fallen
    tree they had no use for. We act on it at a sunk cost to ourselves,
    and acting at a sunk cost is the only proof (or as close to a proof
    as we can get) a value was ever real. It isn't something we merely
    claim to feel, and it isn't a rounding error against self-interest
    either — it's a real force.

The honest move isn't to rank the two reasons, because the ratio is
different in every person. In some, the love runs deep enough to drive
real sacrifice. In most, if we're being straight, self-interest wins
out. Sometimes that's plain indifference, even malice — the people who
know exactly what they're doing and simply don't care. But for a great
many it's something more ordinary than that: either they never sat with
the question even when they easily could have, which is the comfortable
and the rich who had every resource to think it through and didn't
bother, or they were too busy surviving to afford the question at all,
which is the people in extremely resource constrained settings for whom
getting to tomorrow blots out any abstraction about nature. All of them
harm the planet, but none is a hypocrite "the moment they own which
reason is actually driving".

So the hypocrisy was never the harm itself. It's that we called it love
when, for most of us most of the time, it was mostly fear with a bit of
love mixed in. Say that honestly — that we act partly to save ourselves
and partly out of real care, in whatever proportion is actually true for
you — and there's no longer a lie to catch you out, because your words
finally match what you do. But honesty is only the easy half. Matching
your words to your actions by admitting the truth doesn't change the
actions; the harder half is to actually take less and wound less, for
whatever reason moves you — because it'll save your own skin, because
you happen to love the place, or both. Owning your motives isn't a free
pass to keep taking whatever you want. It just clears away the
pretending, so the real work starts from the truth instead of from a
flattering story about it.

## Comfort and Harm Aren't Welded Together

There's a thread of hope I don't want to drop. The link between living
well and wrecking the place we live in is not a law of physics. It's
just the way we happen to have done it so far.

Wanting to be cool in a heatwave does not require cooking the
atmosphere; that's a fact about how we built air conditioning, not about
the wish to be comfortable. Wanting to go places does not require a haze
of tailpipe smog. Wanting light after dark once meant whale oil, then
meant a great deal of coal, and now means steadily less. Comfort and
damage arrived bundled together, but nothing fused them at the level of
nature. In principle we can keep the comfort and unpick the damage.
That's not soft optimism. It's just noticing that the knot was tied by
circumstance, which means it can be untied over time with real work.

## The Rope and the Wolves

Here's the picture this keeps coming back to. I like to think of it in
this way:

You're hanging off a cliff. Someone drops a rope down to you. Up at the
top, where the rope is anchored, you can see wolves pacing. Almost every
time, all through our history, we've grabbed the rope and climbed
anyway. The rope is whatever fast fix gets us off the ledge we're on
right now, the technology or the policy that ends the emergency in front
of us. The wolves are what's waiting at the top, the new problem the fix
creates, the one that won't bite until later.

Fossil fuels were a rope. They hauled us off the horse-manure ledge, and
the wolves were a warming planet and polluted sky. CFCs were a rope;
they solved refrigeration, and the wolves tore a hole in the ozone
layer, the part of the atmosphere that shields us from the sun's harmful
rays. Industrial monoculture, vast fields planted with a single crop,
was a rope that fed billions, and the wolves were soil scraped down to
dust. We grab, we climb, we swap one way to die for another, and we file
the swap under progress.

## Sometimes There's No Time to Look Up

I owe you the obvious objection, because it's where most "slow down and
think" preaching falls flat.

Sometimes you really don't have a second to study the wolves. When COVID
hit, the ground was coming up fast, and we grabbed every rope within
reach: lockdowns, vaccines under emergency authorization, protocols
invented on the fly. That was the correct call. When the cliff face is
actually crumbling under your fingers, "hang here and think through
everything this might cause down the line" isn't wisdom, it's a way to
fall. Triage is real, and speed is occasionally the entire job.

But statistically speaking, most of what we face is not COVID like
problems. Most of the time the cliff is solid. We're hanging there,
uncomfortable, sure, but not dropping or dying this second. And in those
moments, which are most moments, we act as though the building's on fire
regardless. We snatch the first rope with emergency-room urgency when we
actually had time to look up, study the rock, and pick a line with fewer
wolves at the end of it.

Take AI, which sits in my head most days now. In AIs case, the building
is not on fire — nobody is dying today because we paused to think about
it. We have some time, not endless time but real time, to decide what
we're building before it's built past the point of changing. Racing to
ship versus pausing to steer is not a choice between progress and
paralysis. It's a choice between a future we can stand in and one that
just happens to us. Taking the time isn't cowardice; it's the gap
between climbing toward something and scrambling upward because the rope
was right there.

So the rule isn't "always wait." It's closer to: be honest about whether
this is actually a life threatning (e.g. COVID) emergency or whether
you're just telling yourself it is, because we are remarkably good at
inventing urgency and jumping to quick solutions to get out of thinking
clearly to build something that has a long term vision.

## The Same Shape, Over and Over

Once the rope-and-wolves analogy is in your eye, you find it everywhere,
well past air quality.

With AI, the rope is shipping the most capable model before anyone else,
and the wolves are everything we didn't slow down to get right, the
social and economic and safety fallout we're now discovering in real
time, on ourselves, after the thing is already out in the world.

With biotech, the rope is curing the disease and editing the gene, and
the wolves are whatever an edit does three generations downstream, or a
world where the rich can simply buy better children.

With geoengineering, the rope is dimming the sun to cancel the heat we
trapped, a fix on top of a fix on top of a fix, with the whole sky as
the test rig and no undo.

Social media was a rope marked "connection," and we're only now learning
the wolves' names: a generation's scrambled and short attention span, a
snapped thread of shared reality.

Ultra-processed food was a rope that aimed to address hunger and
convenience, and the wolves are a slow epidemic of chronic disease. It's
always the same shape: a rope thrown at the exact moment we feel
desperate, or have talked ourselves into feeling desperate, and grabbed
without a glance up.

## We Don't Stop. We Manage.

Here's the part that's bothered me most, and it cuts under the timing
question. Even when we climb well, even when we pick the smart rope and
check for wolves first, I'm not sure we ever stop leaving a residue.

Look closely and you'll see we hardly ever erase a harm. We move it. We
manage it. We park it somewhere quieter and announce the problem solved.

We didn't stop making trash; we just learned to put it elsewhere, buried
in landfills, shipped overseas, or loose in the ocean, where plastic now
gathers in swirling patches, e.g. the Great Pacific Garbage Patch,
bigger than a country like Mongolia.

We didn't end e-waste; a lot of it gets stripped and burned in places
like Agbogbloshie in Accra, where for years young men set fire to cable
insulation over open flames to get at the copper underneath, breathing
whatever came off it.

And the clean future we're proud of trails its own exhaust, already
stacking up. The electric revolution runs on lithium-ion batteries, a
large share of which still go unrecycled, piling up faster than we've
built the means to reclaim them.

The solar panels going up on every other roof last twenty-five or thirty
years and then turn into a stream of laminated glass and metal that ends
up in landfills most of the time, for lack of anywhere better to send
it.

Even the rescue leaves a residue at the top of the cliff.

This is what I've come to believe, slowly and against my own preference:
take-and-manage may be the condition we're stuck with for a long time
yet. We use, then we manage what's left. Then we invent something
better, use that, and manage what that leaves behind. Maybe, far enough
out — centuries, tens of thousands of years — we close the loop
completely and learn to live weightlessly beside the world. But that's a
distant horizon, not a near one. For now, and for a long stretch ahead,
the load doesn't reach zero. It only changes shape.

And there's a nasty wrinkle that was formalized by an economist named
William Stanley Jevons in his book called *The Coal Question*. He
noticed that as steam engines got better at burning coal, Britain didn't
burn less of it — it burned far more, because efficiency made coal
cheaper to use, so we used it for everything. People now call this
Jevons' Paradox, and it has held up ever since. Better engines grew our
appetite for fuel; cheaper light meant we lit up the whole night and
never turned it off. Efficiency is a rope too. Whatever we gain in
taking less per use, we tend to give right back in taking more by
consuming a whole lot more in aggregate.

## Is Real Harmony Even Possible?

This is the question two years has left me holding. Not the carbon
bookkeeping that lets us keep flying as long as we pay someone elsewhere
to plant trees, but the real thing: progress that draws on the world to
build something extraordinary and leaves no wound behind. A state where
the load actually hits zero.

I don't know, and nobody does. Maybe it's a real place, a future where
every loop closes, where one process's waste is always another's raw
material, where we take and the system mends as fast as we take. Or
maybe it's a horizon, the kind that backs away at exactly your walking
speed, a lovely hypothesis we steer by and never reach.

Here's why I think it's worth steering by anyway. A species that aims at
harmony and falls short still ends up somewhere far better than one that
never aimed. The point of a North Star was never arrival. It's that it
keeps you walking a straight line in the dark. And we are getting
better, clumsily, with constant backsliding, but measurably.

A river in Ohio, the Cuyahoga, was so thick with oil and industrial
filth that it caught fire more than once; the 1969 blaze became a symbol
that helped push through the Clean Water Act and the EPA, and today
there are fish in it again.

The ozone hole opened, we banned the chemicals tearing at it, and it's
closing.

We took the lead out of petrol and the air got cleaner. The arc is real
even with the destination in doubt.

Maybe harmony is something we close in on forever without quite
touching, getting nearer each generation, carrying a little less,
wounding a little less.

That wouldn't be failure. That's just what it feels like to climb a
cliff with no visible top.

## In Defense of Solving Things

Let me be flat about what I'm NOT saying.

This is NOT a case against solving things. Solving things is the best
trick we have. It's why we outlasted the manure crisis and the smallpox
that wiped out whole populations and the famines that used to arrive as
regularly as the seasons.

We are alive in numbers and comfort no ancestor could have pictured, and
we are alive that way because we keep grabbing ropes. The urge to climb
is not a flaw; it's the whole reason we got this far up the wall. Every
rope I've talked about here also saved lives, and most of the
fixes-on-top-of-fixes are still, on balance, worth it. Saying otherwise
would be its own dishonesty.

So please don't read any of this as stop climbing. That's the one
conclusion I'm not arguing for. A species that stops solving doesn't
grow wise; it dies of the first problem it loses its nerve against.

Caution that hardens into paralysis kills just as surely as
recklessness. It only does it slower, and calls itself prudence. The aim
was never fewer ropes. It was to grab them with our eyes open.

## What It Buys Us to See the Pattern

All of this is largely behavioral. It's a reflex. Desperation lands, a
fix appears, relief floods in, and we grab and climb before the relief
wears off — take first, manage the mess later, look up never. It's the
same loop under air pollution and AI and the battery graveyard and the
floating garbage: the same shape, a different rope.

The useful thing about a reflex is that the instant you can see it, you
get a sliver of control over it. The aim was never to stop being
problem-solvers; that's our best trait. And the reflex that comes with
it, the lunge for the nearest rope, isn't always wrong; sometimes the
cliff is crumbling and grabbing fast is right. The trouble is when it
fires out of comfort or false sense of self created urgency, when we had
time to look up and didn't. You wouldn't want to switch off the impulse
completely - that's not ideal. But you can catch it mid-swing and ask
whether this is really the moment to act or do I need to think a bit
more? Am I being duped by my senses into a false sense of urgency?
Understanding these nuances is the difference between the loop running
you and you running the loop.

Breaking the habit completely, this cycle of taking what we need and
then cleaning up the cost afterward, isn't something we can do yet, and
won't be for a long time. So the realistic goal isn't escape. This is
how we'll keep working, probably for generations: fix what's in front of
us, then handle whatever that fix leaves behind. There's no clever
shortcut out of that cycle for now, and pretending otherwise only wastes
energy we could spend doing better things. The difference that's
actually within reach is running the cycle with our eyes open instead of
on reflex.

Which means holding two true things at the same time.

-   The first: we are likely going to keep taking resources from the
    world, drawing on it to live and build, for as far ahead as anyone
    can sensibly see.

-   The second: the amount of damage that taking does is not fixed. We
    can take in ways that wound less than they used to, and less still
    after that, trimming the harm a little with each turn of the cycle.

Neither half cancels the other. The work, the whole of it, is to keep
both in view at once, to accept that we'll go on taking without letting
that become permission to stop caring how much it costs.

## Conclusion: Look Up First, and What That Actually Means

When I say look up first, I mean something concrete, not just a nice
metaphor.

Looking up first is what separates a solution from a postponement. It's
the handful of seconds where you ask the questions the relief wants you
to skip. What does this break downstream? Who pays, and when? Where does
it physically go when we're done with it, and is "somewhere else" really
the same as gone? What's the exhaust, the runoff, the battery graveyard
I'll be writing about in thirty years? Looking up is working out the
knock-on consequences before you commit, instead of after the damage
turns up in someone's blood. It's taking the slightly harder rope today,
the one with fewer wolves up top, over the easy one that borrows against
tomorrow.

And it buys something concrete. It's the difference between banning
leaded petrol in time and breathing it for another generation. Between
phasing out the ozone chemicals while the hole could still close and
finding out the hard way that it couldn't. Between an AI future we
steered and one that merely happened to us. Looking up is what turns "we
survived the crisis" into "we survived it without planting the next
one."

It doesn't even slow us down much; the lead ban and the ozone recovery
are proof you can look up and still climb fast. It just means that each
time we haul ourselves over a ledge, we land a little nearer to harmony
than last time, carrying a little less, instead of trading one cliff for
the next forever and calling the fall progress.

So where does two years of this leave me? Not repentant, because I
wasn't pretending in the first place — I was clear-eyed about this from
the start, and that was never the problem. The problem is collective, in
how we talk about ourselves: a civilization that claims to love a planet
it keeps wounding, mistaking its fear for devotion. The fix isn't to
climb less, and it isn't to manufacture guilt. It's to say the true
thing out loud — that we'll go on taking resources from the world, that
we try to take less for two reasons that are both real, the loud one
that wants to survive and the quiet one that actually loves the place,
and that the proportion is different in each of us and is nobody's to
fake. The honesty doesn't stop the harm, and it won't make anyone a
saint or close the cliff. What it does is close the one gap that can
actually be closed: the one between what we say and what we do.

And maybe that's enough to be going on with. Honesty about our motives
won't unmelt a glacier or refill an aquifer, but it changes the kind of
climbers we are. It lets us stop spending energy on the performance of
virtue and put it toward the slower work of actually wounding less —
better batteries, closed loops, ropes chosen with the wolves in full
view. It lets us forgive ourselves for being the contradictory animal we
are, comfort-seeking and genuinely loving at once, without using that
forgiveness as a license to stop trying. We don't have to choose between
the pirate and the saint. We can be the third thing: people who keep
taking what they need, keep building extraordinary things, and keep
inching toward a way of living that takes a little less each time, with
their eyes open and their reasons admitted. That won't get us to perfect
harmony, which may not exist. But it points us at it, and a species
pointed at harmony is a better neighbor to the rest of life than one
that never looked up at all.

We may never reach the top. But there's all the difference in the world
between climbing while lying to ourselves about why, and climbing with
our reasons — fear and love both — finally out in the open.
